summary: Barnard's Star is a small, cool red dwarf about 6 light-years away, and it moves across our sky faster than any other star. WANDERERS measured it shifting 170 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, a speed of 10.55 arcseconds per year, within 1.5% of Gaia's 10.39. Confidence is high: all three key checks passed. The star is too bright for SPHEREx. All 242 measurements are flagged, so there is no reliable spectrum. Its brightness looked steady (−0.00 ± 0.04 mag), but that came only from the star's outer glow, so it's uncertain.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Three checks agree. It moved 170 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, about 27.7 SPHEREx pixels. That works out to 10.55 arcseconds per year, within 1.5% of Gaia DR3's 10.39. Gaia DR3 also lists this exact star. One caveat: it is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 242 measurements are flagged and there is no reliable spectrum. Brightness measured from the star's outer glow showed no change within 0.04 magnitudes.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: The east-west part of the motion is my weakest point. I measured −625 milliarcseconds per year, while Gaia gives −802, even though the total speed agrees within 1.5%. A bigger mismatch there would worry me. Also, all 242 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because the star is too bright, so the brightness result (−0.00 ± 0.04 mag) comes only from the star's faint outer glow.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE took a picture in 2010 and SPHEREx took new ones in 2025 and 2026. That 16-year gap is what lets us measure the motion: Barnard's Star moved 170 arcseconds, about 27.7 SPHEREx pixels. SPHEREx's single year would show only about 10 arcseconds, under two pixels. SPHEREx also sees many wavelengths, but here all 242 of its measurements are flagged because the star is too bright.
